newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Gas game heats up between Ukraine, Russian Gazprom.
newsitem.headline: Gas game heats up between Ukraine, Russian Gazprom.

text.p: Ukraine and Russian gas monopoly RAO Gazprom are caught in a complex game of supply cuts, urgent meetings and secretive commercial talks -- all overshadowed by suspicions of Moscow's imperialistic intentions.

Gazprom chief Rem Vyakhirev held talks in Kiev on Wednesday with President Leonid Kuchma, his prime minister and the upper echelons of the State Oil and Gas Committee after his company cut supplies by one-third to Ukraine this week.

Gazprom said after talks that natural gas supplies to Ukraine would be cut back because of huge debts, but at the same time promised to help its neighbouring former Soviet republic build up strategic gas resources.
Frustrated by countries not paying, Gazprom also cut flows to Belarus by 50 percent before resuming them on Wednesday.
Ukraine owes Gazprom $3.5 billion for 1992-94 supplies, including $1.4 billion already restructured for 12 years with the first $221.5 million tranche to be paid by the end of 1997.

Gazprom's statement said despite cuts to the two largest privately-owned Ukrainian importers, the company would continue to supply gas under an existing contract so Ukraine's strategic resources could keep running.

Ukraine has allowed private traders to import and move Russian gas since 1995, but the system has not improved bad payments records, with United Energy Systems of Ukraine (UESU) and Intergaz each owing Gazprom $150 million.
Vyakhirev and Kuchma agreed to keep the current gas distribution system via private commercial companies and not return to using only state-owned Ukrgazprom.
According to energy sources, Vyakhirev held unannounced talks in Kiev with heads of several gas trading firms, who greeted him at the airport alongside government officials.

Sceptics said that despite declarations about market mechanisms and involvement of non-state companies, Ukraine's energy market is still heavily dependent on protection from the government and personal ties with the government and Gazprom.
"Relations are personal because relations between major businesses like these are always personal," said Nikita Poturayev, a spokesman for UESU, which last year reported turnover of $10 billion.

Some observers said the Russian government's financial pressure on Gazprom forced the giant to take a tougher line in dealing with its foreign consumers and to try to make Ukraine reduce transit tariffs for moving Russian gas to Europe.
Ukraine, the world's single largest consumer and conveyor of Russian gas, is due this year to import 53 billion cubic metres and to transport about 125 billion cubic metres.
Gazprom pays Ukraine not in cash but about with about 30 bcm of Russian gas annually.

"By cutting supplies Vyakhirev is trying to force Ukraine to reduce transit tariffs. They blame the high tariffs for making Russian gas expensive in Europe. But in fact Russian gas is cheaper than Norwegian or Dutch gas," said Vitaly Knyazhansky, an energy commentator at the Den daily.

Some officials in both Ukraine and Belarus, countries dominated by Moscow for more than three centuries and living independently for just six years, still think Russia is heavily influenced by politics in its economic dealings.
Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko complained the cuts in supplies were made by "opponents of Belarussian-Russian integration" and his Russian "enemies".
Volodymyr Maxymiv, a top Ukrgazprom official, accused Gazprom of showing unhappiness over Ukrainian independence.

"Commercial relations between Gazprom and customers are heavily influenced by geopolitical factors. Gazprom became the main instrument of Moscow's geopolitics a long time ago," Moscow's daily Izvestia wrote on Thursday.
